title: When a price change raises or lowers revenue and margin
reading_md:
**What it is.** A price cut raises revenue only if demand is elastic, and even then profit can fall, because each unit earns less. So judge a price change on contribution, not revenue. The break-even volume change, from Nagle and Müller's break-even analysis, says how far volume must move to keep contribution where it was. Elasticity is explained in the reading **Own-price elasticity**, and margin terms in **Gross margin and markup**.

**How to work it out.**

Revenue = P × Q. Contribution = (P - unit cost) × Q.

Break-even volume change: %ΔQ = -ΔP / (CM + ΔP), where CM is the unit contribution margin before the change.

Worked example. Price €10 to €9, units 1,000 to 1,200, unit cost €6.

- Revenue: 10 × 1,000 = €10,000 becomes 9 × 1,200 = €10,800 (+8.0%).
- Contribution: (10 - 6) × 1,000 = €4,000 becomes (9 - 6) × 1,200 = €3,600 (-10.0%).
- Break-even: -(-1) / (4 - 1) = 1/3, a volume rise of 33.3% (1 decimal).
- In units: 1,000 × 4/3 = 1,333.3, rounded up to 1,334, the smallest whole number of units that does not lose contribution.

Say which one you give: the break-even percentage (33.3%) or the units, rounded up (1,334). The cut needed 1,334 units and got 1,200: revenue rose, contribution fell.

**In the interview.** "Why do low-margin products need huge volume gains from a discount?" A model answer: "The discount is a large share of a small margin. With a €4 margin, a €1 cut takes a quarter of it, so volume must rise by a third just to stand still."

**Common mistakes.**

- Judging a price cut on revenue only.
- Assuming inelastic demand means the price can rise without limit. Elasticity changes along the demand curve, and customers and rivals react.
- Ignoring competitor reaction and the long-run loss of customers.
